content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.85. I used 51 of the 60 budget points.

**Design:** I used the free `compare` command to find tasks where the two hypotheses predict different costs. Swapping a single rule can drop output overlap to 0, and a task with all three rules new can still overlap a trained task by 0.56. So "how many rules are new" and "how similar the outputs are" can be pulled apart.

**Evidence:** Lower numbers mean the learner needed fewer examples.

| Trained on | Test task | New rules | Peak overlap with a trained task | Mean examples (n) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M1 | L1-S1-M2 | 1 | 0 | ~30 (6) |
| L1-S1-M1 | L3-S4-M3 | 3 | 0 | ~33 (6) |
| L1-S1-M1 | L3-S3-M4 | 3 | 0.56 | ~46 (6) |
| + L2-S2-M2 | L2-S1-M1 | 0 | 0.56 | 13.6 (7) |
| + L2-S2-M2 | L1-S1-M2 | 0 | 0.375 | 16.8 (4) |
| + L2-S2-M2 | L3-S3-M4 | 3 | 0.56 | 35 (7) |
| + L2-S2-M2 | L3-S4-M3 | 3 | 0.19 | 43 (4) |

- **Matched pair:** L2-S1-M1 and L3-S3-M4 overlap a trained task equally (0.5625). The one built from familiar rules was cheaper by about 21 examples.
- **Becoming familiar:** L1-S1-M2 fell from about 30 to 17 once its last new rule was covered by training. The all-new tasks did not get cheaper.
- **Overlap didn't help:** in the first phase, the all-new task with the highest output overlap was the most expensive.

**Caveats:**
- The tests are very noisy (single results ranged from 1 to 67, spread about 15).
- I ran only 3 untrained baseline tests per task. Tasks differ in difficulty even before training, and those baselines are rough.
- I can't rule out a holistic learner whose hidden similarity measure happens to track shared rules rather than outputs. That is why I gave 0.85 and not higher.
